title: Cadence and the Slipping Note
markdown:
Every grand adventure begins with a note, and Cadence’s world was the cello’s deep wood-and-string one. He was skilled, and more than that he was sure. Never wrong about tempo, never wrong about which notes belonged together, never wrong about pitch. Dark hair fell into his eyes when he worked; the hair was the only thing allowed to be messy. Sun through the music-room windows laid long shadows that kept time with his bow. Rosin dusted the floor in a faint gold. The cello had been a friend for years. He treated it as if friendship required being right.

Bartholomew, the school’s administrative ghost, kept spectral dust motes in order and phantom bookshelves aligned. He wanted things proper. A see-through outline in a neat spectral tie, phantom quill over phantom ledgers, he watched Cadence’s practice with detached amusement and a faint knowing that did not interrupt. When a chair was left at an angle, Bartholomew sighed without breath and nudged it true.

A tiny ripple arrived in the otherwise perfect afternoon. The piece was old, brittle, smelling of forgotten lavender, fetched from the deepest archives where even Bartholomew’s filing grew shy. A sweet tune, the kind that usually made Cadence smile before he had finished the first bar. One repeating A, though, seemed off—not flat. Slipping. One moment it was an A from the 1950s, clear, edged. The next it wore the warmer roundness of the 1970s, a mellow hug. Cadence played it again. And again. He checked the pegs. He checked the weather in the room, which was only sun. Certainty wavered like a candle in a draft. A note was a note. There was no slipping. He was not wrong. His ears, usually allies, disagreed with his mind.

“Bartholomew.” Frustration kept small, as if naming it would make it official. The ghost arrived silent, tie straight. “This A. Does it sound odd? Does it shift?”

Bartholomew tilted, a shimmer. He listened with the patience of someone who had filed a century of bells. “Odd is subjective, Master Cadence. Harmonic resonance sits within acceptable changes in time. Faint fluctuations. Echoes.”

“Changes in time? Echoes? The past playing tricks.” He hated not knowing. He hated, more, the suggestion that the page might not be the last word.

They went to the archives: dusty papers, spectral notes, old student projects with names faded to polite ghosts of ink. Bartholomew insisted on a proper route, which meant three wrong turns and one apology to a cabinet. A diary of the same lesson, the handwriting aging and growing younger as they watched, as if the writer were living time backward. Cadence read a sentence that thanked a teacher who had not yet been hired. A photograph of the courtyard in which trees were bare and in leaf at once, winter and June sharing one sky. Each find was a slightly different version of what had happened. Catching a whisper in a storm. Pinning a melody that kept changing key. Cadence’s bow-hand wanted a single answer. Bartholomew wanted a tidy folder. Neither got one.

“The whole school is playing musical chairs with time,” Cadence said, cello forgotten for a moment against his knee. “Or a messy ghost rearranging the timeline.” Bartholomew muttered about misplaced spectral ink, phantom erasures, stationery that aged and de-aged. Untidy. He disapproved of untidy more than of mystery, which was saying something for an administrator.

The search led them to a narrow cobbled lane behind the school, a place the timetables forgot, weeds, damp earth, the ghost of old rain. Nobody practised here; the walls still remembered scales anyway. Air hummed as if a string had been left ringing. Light flickered as through water. Time-echoes were strongest here: phantom footsteps overlapping, fading, returning. Cadence heard younger versions of his own steps, quick, then older ones, thoughtful, all at once. He asked about the music’s start; Bartholomew answered with facts from ten years before he had been a ghost, a voice from a ledger Cadence had not opened. Funhouse mirrors. “Impossible. We keep meeting older or younger versions of the truth. It’s chaos.”

In that lane they found the heart of it: not a glitch. A faint spectral echo of a girl no older than Cadence, brow furrowed, violin in small hands, struggling with the same A. She was trying to catch a feeling just beyond reach. No perfect pitch. No spectral ledgers. A wish to make the note hers—the sadness of a darkening sky, wind in trees. She held it until it felt right, even if it was not exactly as written. Heartfelt, a small defiance of the page. The echo did not look at them. It was busy being brave.

Bartholomew’s voice went softer than Cadence had heard it, a spectral kind of understanding that did not come with a stamp. That attempt had rippled. The A was a little more alive for everyone who came after. Not a mistake. A human weather that had got into the music.

Cadence stood. Cobbles solid under school shoes. Damp earth. He thought of his need to be right, of Bartholomew who had filed countless ordinary magnificent hours and still could not make this one sit square. He did not make a speech. He raised the cello without looking at the music, listened to the lane and the girl’s lingering echo, and played the A as it was in that moment—not 1950s, not 1970s, not the score. The air settled, a contented sigh that might have been wind. Light steadied, warm, as if time had found a bar of rest. Bartholomew felt, for the first time in his spectral bookkeeping, something like pride, a faint warmth in a chest that did not strictly exist.

Cadence still aimed for precision after that. He also left room, in the same bar, for a note that had been brave before it was correct. Bartholomew filed the lane under a heading he invented and did not show the headteacher: not a mess. A record worth keeping crooked.
characters: Cadence (young musician who notices time behaving oddly), Bartholomew (a local ghost who is mostly administrative)
audience: children aged 11-12, fantastic mystery adventure for older children
